issues.legal_issue: The validity of a will challenged on suspicious circumstances depends on the cumulative assessment of the circumstances surrounding its execution, rather than the effect of any single circumstance.
material_facts: The will excluded the testator’s sons and left property to her daughter and granddaughter, stating reasons for that disposition.
A prior will had substantially identical contents, and the reasons for excluding the sons were apparent from the will.

The daughter participated in arranging the will’s execution and registration, and the testator’s friend attested it; the Court found these circumstances did not warrant an adverse conclusion in the context of the earlier will and the evidence.
The original will was missing from the testator’s custody, and the explanation that it was lost before her death was not disbelieved merely because no police report had been made.

The discrepancy concerning the place of execution was explained by the use of a standard verification form, and evidence described the Sub-Registrar’s usual practice of ascertaining or explaining the will’s contents to the testator.
The other unusual circumstances, including the changed attesting witnesses and the non-examination of one attesting witness, were found capable of explanation.
issues.conclusion: The suspicious circumstances did not justify rejecting the will; the High Court was right to accept it as valid.
issues.legal_principle: A court must scrutinize unusual features and suspicious circumstances surrounding a will and assess their cumulative effect; no single feature or circumstance is determinative. The Court applied the principles in H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Bharpur Singh v. Shamsher Singh, Rani Purnima Debi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Deb, Apoline D’souza v. John D’souza, Pentakota Satyanarayana v. Pentakota Seetharatnam, Mahesh Kumar v. Vinod Kumar, and Ved Mitra Verma v. Dharam Deo Verma. Sections 281 and 282 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, were referred to in connection with the verification accompanying the probate petition.

rule.if: will_validity_contested and suspicious_circumstances_present and circumstances_reasonably_explained and will_contents_clear_and_reasons_apparent

predicates.will_validity_contested: A party to a proceeding disputing a will challenges whether it was validly executed.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_present: The will’s features or the circumstances surrounding its execution appear unusual or suspicious.
predicates.circumstances_reasonably_explained: The evidence provides reasonable explanations for the unusual features and circumstances when they are assessed together.
predicates.will_contents_clear_and_reasons_apparent: The will clearly expresses the testator’s disposition and makes its reasons apparent.

issues.definition: When a will is challenged and suspicious circumstances are reasonably explained in light of its clear contents and apparent reasons, the will is accepted as valid.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court’s jurisdiction on appeal by special leave does not ordinarily permit it to reopen factual findings made by a High Court acting as an appellate court.
material_facts: The appeals by special leave challenged a High Court Division Bench judgment reversing the trial court’s factual assessment of the will.
The High Court had considered the circumstances, evidence, and arguments before reversing the trial court’s findings.
The Supreme Court found no serious question of law requiring debate and no wholly unacceptable factual conclusion demonstrating a travesty of justice.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court would not reappreciate or reopen the High Court’s factual findings, and dismissed the appeals.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court exercises a highly circumscribed jurisdiction on an appeal brought by special leave. It should not reopen factual determinations made by a High Court acting as a first or second appellate court unless those determinations raise a serious question of law or disclose wholly unacceptable factual conclusions that plainly demonstrate a travesty of justice.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_appellate_fact: A party brings an appeal by special leave challenging factual findings made by a High Court acting as an appellate court.
predicates.serious_question_of_law: The challenged factual findings give rise to a serious question of law requiring judicial debate.
predicates.plainly_unacceptable_factfinding: The challenged factual findings are wholly unacceptable and plainly demonstrate a travesty of justice.

issues.definition: When a special-leave appeal challenges appellate factual findings and neither a serious question of law nor plainly unacceptable factfinding is present, those findings are not reopened.
